# Brakes spongy after pad change

A spongy brake pedal following a pad replacement on a Hilux is almost universally a hydraulic system issue, not a suspension one. The immediate symptomâfluid rising above the maximum mark on the reservoirâconfirms that volume has entered the master cylinder from somewhere else in the circuit. When you start the car and get one normal press before the sponginess kicks in, you are witnessing the air bubbles being pushed down into the calipers by that initial stroke. Once the pedal hits the bottom of its travel, those compressible gases return to the reservoir or expand, causing the loss of feel on subsequent presses.

The root cause is almost certainly incomplete bleeding or trapped air introduced during the pad swap. Brake fluid is hygroscopic and slightly compressible under high pressure compared to hydraulic oil, but it contains dissolved air that comes out of solution when the system is opened. If you did not follow a strict bleeding sequence, or if you left the bleeder valve open too long without clamping the line back up, air can migrate into the reservoir. As soon as you open the bleed nut, you create a path of least resistance for air to enter the master cylinder whenever the pedal is released.

### The Bleeding Sequence Matters

You cannot simply attach a clear hose and pump the pedal until no bubbles appear. That approach often fails because it ignores the physics of gas expansion. Air in the lines expands as pressure drops, pulling more air into the system when you release the pedal. To fix this, you need to use a vacuum bleed kit or a pressure bleeder that maintains positive pressure on the reservoir side while evacuating the caliper. This prevents air from being sucked back in through the open bleeder valve.

If you are doing this manually with two people, the person at the wheel must hold firm pressure on the pedal and keep it depressed while you tighten the bleeder valve before releasing the pedal slowly. If you release the pedal first, the vacuum created in the line will suck air back up into the master cylinder reservoir. This is a common mistake that turns a simple pad change into an extended bleeding job.

### Fluid Level and Reservoir Capacity

The fact that your fluid level has risen above the max mark indicates that the total volume of fluid plus air in the system exceeds the reservoir's design capacity. Modern brake systems rely on a specific fluid-to-air ratio within the master cylinder chamber. When you introduce significant amounts of air, the effective hydraulic height drops even if the liquid level looks high.

Before attempting to bleed again, ensure the reservoir is filled with fresh DOT 3 or DOT 4 fluid (whichever your Hilux requires) up to the "Max" line, not overfilled. Overfilling can cause fluid to be pushed out of the master cylinder seals when the pedal is depressed, leading to external leaks and air ingestion. Always check for proper seal compression on the master cylinder; if the rubber diaphragm is damaged or worn, it may allow fluid to bypass into the reservoir during pedal depression, creating a false high-level reading and a spongy feel.

### Verifying System Integrity

If bleeding with correct technique does not restore firm pedal travel, inspect the caliper slides and pistons. A seized caliper piston can prevent proper fluid displacement, mimicking air in the lines. Additionally, check for external leaks at the wheel cylinders or caliper mounts. If a seal is leaking internally but holding pressure temporarily, it will eventually fail catastrophically once the air dissolves enough fluid to lose hydraulic integrity.

There is no software configuration or code fix for this; it requires mechanical intervention and strict adherence to bleeding protocols. If you lack the equipment to perform a vacuum bleed, taking the vehicle to a shop with a pressure bleeder is often faster than troubleshooting manual leaks and air pockets yourself.
